body.x: Nobody's first year of marriage looks like the wedding day, and nobody's looks like the warnings either. What it actually looks like is negotiation — hundreds of small ones, about sleep and laundry and whose mother to visit on Friday — between two people raised in different houses. Most of what makes the first year hard is not a lack of love; it is discovering that your spouse's 'normal' is not yours, in matters so ordinary neither of you knew they were decisions. The couples who do well are rarely the ones who avoid friction. They are the ones who build, early and deliberately, the habits that absorb it.

Start with the unglamorous truth: most early friction is logistical. One of you is a morning person; the other comes alive at midnight. One expects the kitchen reset every night; the other genuinely does not see the dishes. One wants guests every weekend; the other needs the house quiet to recover from the week. None of these is a character flaw, and treating them as one is how small differences harden into contempt. The fix is boring and effective: say the preference out loud, as a preference. 'In my house, we…' is information; silence followed by resentment is a slow leak. In the first months, divide the household's work explicitly — cooking, cleaning, laundry, bills, groceries — by who minds what least, and revisit the division every few months. It removes a hundred future arguments before they happen.
Money: build one system before it builds itself

Money disagreements in year one are rarely about amounts; they are about surprises. Two incomes or one, separate accounts or joint, different instincts about saving — all workable, provided both of you can see the whole picture. What does not work is discovery: the loan a spouse learns about in month eight. Sit down in the first month, with the numbers open, and settle the architecture together:

How will income be held — one joint account, separate accounts, or a shared account for household costs alongside personal ones?
Who pays what, and what counts as a household expense rather than a personal one?
What support will each of you give your parents, and is it a fixed amount you both know?
Above what figure does a purchase need two yeses?
How will you handle khums and charitable giving? Set your khums date and build the habit together, early.
What debts exist, in full, and what is the plan for them?
You will not settle all of it in one sitting, and the system will change as jobs and children change it. What matters is that it is one system, with no locked drawers in it.
In-laws: closeness, with a door that closes

Both of you have gained a family — more duas, more support, more people at the majlis who are yours. It also needs one deliberate protection: the new household must be allowed to be a household. Agree the rhythm of visits and calls between yourselves first; treat both families with visible even-handedness, especially at Eid and in Muharram; and hold one firm line — disagreements are not reported home. The moment an argument is retold to a parent, it stops being between two people and becomes a matter between families, remembered long after the two of you have forgotten it. Present a united front not because you always agree, but because the disagreement belongs to you. The door that closes is what makes the open door possible.

You will argue in the first year — about the negotiations above, and about things too small to list. Treat the friction as information, not verdict: it is two upbringings meeting. What separates couples who argue well is not calmness; it is repair. Keep a few rules between you. No audience: never argue in front of family, and never recruit them afterwards. No contempt: you may attack the problem — the budget, the rota, the plan — but not each other's worth, family or faith. No archaeology: this argument is about this thing, not everything since the wedding. And when it is over, let it be over quickly, with no residue of score-keeping. If you said the cruel thing, apologise for the cruel thing specifically. 'Sorry you felt hurt' is not an apology; 'I should not have said that about your mother' is.
A shared religious life, built deliberately

At the wedding, your faith was celebrated publicly; in the first year it becomes private and practical, and needs the same deliberateness as the money. Pray together sometimes — not as a performance or a check on each other, but because a Maghrib prayed side by side quietly resets the temperature of a house. Go to majlis together, and talk about what you heard on the way home — a shared inner life, not just a shared address. Your first Ramadan together will set patterns that last decades: who wakes for suhoor, how iftar is shared between your home and both families, how you spend the nights of Qadr. Decide these kindly and early. And hold the line on scorekeeping. The moment one spouse becomes the other's religious inspector, worship turns into a battleground. Encourage, invite, model — then leave the account between your spouse and Allah where it belongs.
When to bring in a third person

Almost every couple needs, at some point, a wiser head than either of theirs — and the first year is not too early. Consider seeking counsel when the same argument returns month after month with nothing learned; when silence stretches into days; when money is being hidden in either direction; when family interference has outgrown both of you; or when one of you is unhappy in a way that is not lifting. Who to go to depends on the problem: a scholar you both respect for religious questions, an elder both families trust for family friction, a professional counsellor — there is no shame in it, and increasingly no rarity either — for the patterns between the two of you. Going early, while you both still want the same outcome, is what makes counsel work.

A year from the wedding, couples doing well describe the same discovery: the marriage stopped feeling like two families' project and started feeling like their own small household, with its own rhythms, jokes and ways of praying. That is not the end of the negotiation — it is the negotiation working. Build the habits early, repair quickly, and year one becomes what it should be: not the hardest year, just the first.

excerpt: The first year of marriage is where two upbringings negotiate one household — practical, warm advice on rhythms, money, in-laws, arguments, faith, and knowing when to ask for help.
